target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is ethically acceptable because schools can use animals that are already dead or are food-industry byproducts.
objection: AG2 says the real sourcing pipeline is harmful: roughly 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity, and even “already dead” use still incentivizes a supply chain that harms ecosystems.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is educationally valuable and necessary for biology learning.
objection: AG2 argues dissection is not required for AP Biology or NGSS, and that no U.S. or Canadian medical schools use animals for physician training, so it is hard to justify as a default educational practice.

target: AG1’s claim that real-animal dissection teaches more effectively than alternatives.
objection: AG2 objects that synthetic models, simulations, and virtual dissections teach anatomy equally well or better, and can do so safely and without harming animals.

target: AG1’s idea that sourcing problems are fixed by better procurement rules rather than by ending dissection.
objection: AG2 says regulating sourcing does not remove the underlying harm because classroom demand still incentivizes supply chains, verification is difficult for schools, and the worst-case problem of wild-caught animals remains.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches unique hands-on wet-lab skills that alternatives cannot match.
objection: AG2 says students can develop the same core skills—spatial understanding, observation, labeling, and inquiry—through high-quality models and virtual tools, so dead animals are not needed for those competencies.

target: AG1’s waste-diversion framing for using already-dead or byproduct animals.
objection: AG2 argues that calling specimens “waste” does not remove the moral or ecological problem, because classroom demand still creates incentives that can increase breeding, harvesting, or collection, and origin verification is unreliable.

target: AG1’s proposal to fix sourcing rather than ban dissection.
objection: AG2 invokes a precautionary response: when the practice is tied to animal death and ecosystem impacts, and verification is difficult, the better policy is to avoid dissection entirely rather than rely on enforcement that may miss exceptions.

target: AG1’s equity argument that banning dissection would hurt underfunded schools most.
objection: AG2 responds that equity does not override ethics or environmental harm; if schools need tools, the solution is funding alternatives and training, not continuing animal dissection as the default accessible option.

target: AG1’s idea that opt-in or parallel dissection options make the practice acceptable.
objection: AG2 says “opt-out” or “parallel” arrangements often do not function as real voluntariness in schools because students are still pressured by grades, pacing, and classroom norms, so the harm cannot be reliably limited to willing participants.

target: AG1’s claim that making dissection a separately graded elective lab solves the coercion problem.
objection: AG2 argues that consent from minors in a school setting is not meaningfully voluntary because of institutional authority, and that even limited dissection is unnecessary when alternatives can meet the same AP/NGSS goals without animal death.

target: AG1’s claim that most specimens are already deceased meat-industry byproducts, so dissection does not add harm.
objection: AG2 says byproducts still come from animals killed for food and are not morally neutral, and that even if many specimens are byproducts, purchasing them still creates marginal demand and uncertain supply-chain incentives.

target: AG1’s claim that non-punitive opt-out and parallel assignments remove the ethical problem.
objection: AG2 says opt-out remains socially stigmatizing even without grade penalties, so students may still feel pressure or unequal standing, making participation less than truly voluntary.

target: AG1’s proposal to use waste-only procurement, contractual quantity caps, and same-room parallel stations.
objection: AG2 argues that schools cannot truly verify what enters a “waste stream,” suppliers still have incentives to route more animals into the market, and quantity caps or documentation do not eliminate the risk that dissection increases throughput.

target: AG1’s argument that preservatives and hazardous waste concerns can be solved through standard lab safety protocols.
objection: AG2 replies that safety controls only manage exposure; preservatives and hazardous waste still create environmental and public-health burdens, and many schools lack the staffing, training, or budget to implement those controls consistently.

target: AG1’s proposal to allow dissection only in certified, well-resourced labs or through certified vendors.
objection: AG2 says certification may reduce risk but does not make dissection necessary, and centralized vendors still create market demand for animal parts without eliminating sourcing concerns.

target: AG1’s claim that if specimens are meat-industry byproducts, classroom demand is mostly decoupled from breeding or slaughter.
objection: AG2 argues that even if specimens are byproducts, dissection still uses animal death as the instructional method when effective alternatives exist, so decoupling does not remove the ethical objection.

target: AG1’s claim that real specimens provide uniquely valuable hands-on learning.
objection: AG2 says alternatives can sometimes outperform fixed specimens because virtual and 3D tools allow repeated layered exploration, rotation, zooming, and comparison without tissue degradation or irreversible damage, so real organs are not irreplaceable.

target: AG1’s claim that specimen variation is just a manageable quality issue rather than a reason to avoid dissection.
objection: AG2 responds that variability and inconsistent learning outcomes further weaken the case for dissection, because a non-animal alternative can be both more consistent and ethically preferable.
